sources.citation: Crump, Desmond (Indigenous Languages Coordinator, Queensland Memory). 2015. Aboriginal names mostly of marine animals from North Queensland. State Library of Queensland blog (Indigenous languages), 19 August 2015. [Describes and reproduces image extracts of Whitley, G.P. 1936, Mankind 2(2): 42-44, the c.100-word Ngaro / 'Whitsunday Passage' wordlist from Mugera (Billy McKenzie) and Frank Dewar, Lindeman Island, 1933; notes a scanned copy lodged with Mackay Regional Library.]
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone. Language content is limited to single words quoted from Whitley 1936 (dairbaia 'whiting', winta 'ironbark canoe', Yara-kimber/Yarrakiemmea 'Lindeman Island, meaning snapper fish', 'a choice of five words for stingray') and the remark that Ngaro 'was not well documented and there may be minimal resources, if any'; the embedded images are extracts of Whitley's printed list (English gloss - native name), i.e. wordlist-only data.

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 2009. The Biri dialects and their neighbours. Transactions of the Royal Society of South Australia 133(2): 219-256.
sources.note: The only modern treatment of Giya (p. 246: relation to Biri/Wirri, the initial /gi/ of Giya and githi 'spear'); comparative reworking of the Curr lists, so a stress statement is unlikely but it is the one place a linguist has written about Giya's sound shape.

sources.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1983. Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland. Pacific Linguistics D-54. Canberra: ANU.
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7091.Q4 H65 1983
sources.note: a full-text search for stress/accent Giya/Gia/Kia/Proserpine: no Giya material at all (its 'Bowen language' is Birri). Its group-wide remark that stress is not distinctive with a tendency to stress the second syllable applies to the Gunggari-group languages Holmer recorded, not to Giya.

sources.citation: Roth, Walter E. 1910. North Queensland Ethnography. Bulletin No. 18. Social and individual nomenclature. Records of the Australian Museum 8(1): 79-106.
sources.note: No phonology content. The only Giya-relevant sentence (p. 83): '..it may be indicated by its place of origin—thus, Yuro-Kappa, Kia-Kappa, and Yilbar-Kappa denote the Bowen, Proserpine, and Charters Towers languages respectively'. No Giya forms, no remarks on pronunciation.

sources.citation: Curr, Edward. 1887. No. 146. Scrubby Creek. In E. M. Curr, The Australian Race, vol. III, pp. 42-43. Melbourne: John Ferres. (Glottolog tags it 'Scrubby Creek = Biri or Giya'; ozbib: 'vocabulary unidentified by Oates & Oates'.)
sources.note: Nothing; another unmarked amateur wordlist (woorra 'kangaroo', kundooloo 'emu', yamba 'camp'), no accent marks, no prose on pronunciation; attribution to Giya is itself uncertain.

sources.citation: Shea, Sergeant B. 1887. No. 136. From Port Denison to Cape Gloucester. In E. M. Curr, The Australian Race, vol. III, pp. 4-7 (vocabulary pp. 6-7). Melbourne: John Ferres, Government Printer.
sources.note: Nothing. A c. 120-item wordlist of the 'Bumbarra tribe' (Port Denison to Cape Gloucester, inland to the head of the Proserpine River) in English amateur spelling (rooa 'kangaroo', koolachu 'opossum', goondooloo 'emu', githa 'war-spear', yamba 'camp'); no accent marks (checked on the page scan at 110 dpi), and Curr's two pages of prose (pp. 4-5) discuss customs and a few lexical mergers, not pronunciation. This is the only primary record of Giya (AUSTLANG: 'all that remains for this language', citing Terrill 1998:87).

sources.citation: South Australian Museum Archives. Tindale collection (AA 338), language-group catalogue entry 'Gia (QLD)': location, refs 'Shea in Curr, 1887; Roth, 1903; Davidson, 1938; Tindale, 1938 MS, 1940', alternative names Kia, Bumbara, Bumbarra; inventory AA 338/1/15/1 (1938-39 expedition journal I), AA 338/1/37 (Barrinean journal 1938 / Palm Island 1963), maps.
sources.note: Catalogue record only; no linguistic content online. The journals (AA 338/1/15/1) are not digitised on this page; even if they hold a few Gia words they would be unanalysed field jottings, not a description.
